prism-2015-01.title: Halving
prism-2015-01.body:
Each term is half of the one before: $64\to32\to16\to8\to4$. The next term is $4\div2 = 2$.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prism-2015-01.title: Powers of 2
prism-2015-01.body:
The terms are $2^6, 2^5, 2^4, 2^3, 2^2$; the exponent drops by 1 each time, so next is $2^1 = 2$.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prism-2015-02.title: Digit sums
prism-2015-02.body:
A number is divisible by 3 exactly when its digit sum is. Digit sums: $9$, $1+8=9$, $2+8=10$, $3+6=9$, $4+5=9$. Only 28 has a digit sum (10) not divisible by 3.

**Answer: (C) 28**

prism-2015-03.title: Follow the cars
prism-2015-03.body:
Andrew gives 2 cars and Liam gives 3, so the boys keep $2+3 = 5$ cars between them. Elizabeth then has $n + 5$, which must equal $2\times5 = 10$. So $n = 5$.

**Answer: (C) 5**

prism-2015-03.title: Check the choices
prism-2015-03.body:
After the gifts the boys have 5 cars, so Elizabeth must end with 10. She receives 5, so she started with $10 - 5 = 5$. (E.g. $n=10$ would give her 15, too many.)

**Answer: (C) 5**

prism-2015-04.title: Simultaneous equations
prism-2015-04.body:
Let Mary be $M$ and Tom $T = M+2$. Then $M + (M+2) = 20$, so $2M = 18$, $M = 9$ and $T = 11$. The product is $9\times11 = 99$.

**Answer: (A) 99**

prism-2015-04.title: Think about the middle
prism-2015-04.body:
Two numbers that add to 20 and differ by 2 sit 1 on either side of their average 10: they are 9 and 11. Product: $(10-1)(10+1) = 100 - 1 = 99$.

**Answer: (A) 99**

prism-2015-05.title: New unit prices
prism-2015-05.body:
One bar costs €0.50; after a 10% rise it costs €0.55. One cake costs €2.10 ÷ 3 = €0.70; after a 10% drop it costs €0.63. So 3 bars and 2 cakes cost $3\times0.55 + 2\times0.63 = 1.65 + 1.26 = $ €2.91.

**Answer: (A) €2.91**

prism-2015-05.title: Old cost, then adjust
prism-2015-05.body:
At the old prices, 3 bars cost €1.50 and 2 cakes cost €1.40. Bars go up by 10% of €1.50 = 15 cent; cakes go down by 10% of €1.40 = 14 cent. New total: $2.90 + 0.15 - 0.14 = $ €2.91.

**Answer: (A) €2.91**

prism-2015-06.title: Check each statement
prism-2015-06.body:
(1) $4 + 8 = 12 \ne 32$: false.

(2) $4(3\times1 - 2) = 4\times1 = 4$: true.

(3) $\frac13+\frac13 = \frac23 \ne \frac32$: false.

(4) $\frac1{21} < \frac1{20}$, so $\frac1{20}+\frac1{21} < \frac1{20}+\frac1{20} = \frac1{10}$: true.

Exactly two are true.

**Answer: (C)**

prism-2015-06.title: Statement (4) exactly
prism-2015-06.body:
For (4) one can also compute $\frac1{20}+\frac1{21} = \frac{41}{420}$, while $\frac1{10} = \frac{42}{420}$, so it is true. Together with (2) true and (1), (3) false, exactly two statements hold.

**Answer: (C)**

prism-2015-07.title: Raise to the 12th power
prism-2015-07.body:
Raising positive numbers to the 12th power keeps their order. $(\sqrt2)^{12} = 2^6 = 64$, $(\sqrt[3]3)^{12} = 3^4 = 81$, $(\sqrt[4]4)^{12} = 4^3 = 64$. So $\sqrt[3]3$ is the largest of the roots. Now compare it with $\frac32$ by cubing: $\left(\frac32\right)^3 = \frac{27}{8} = 3.375 > 3$, so $\frac32 > \sqrt[3]3$. Clearly $\frac32 > 1$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac32$**

prism-2015-07.title: Estimate
prism-2015-07.body:
$\sqrt[4]4 = \sqrt{\sqrt4} = \sqrt2 \approx 1.414$. $\sqrt[3]3 \approx 1.442$ because $1.44^3 \approx 2.99$ and $1.45^3 \approx 3.05$. Both are less than $1.5$: indeed $1.5^2 = 2.25 > 2$ and $1.5^3 = 3.375 > 3$. So $\frac32$ is the greatest.

**Answer: (B) $\frac32$**

prism-2015-08.title: Inclusion–exclusion
prism-2015-08.body:
$200 - 60 = 140$ students are male or study Art (or both). Adding the males and the Art students, $100 + 100 = 200$, counts the overlap twice, so the overlap is $200 - 140 = 60$.

**Answer: (C) 60**

prism-2015-08.title: Venn diagram
prism-2015-08.body:
Let $x$ be the number of male Art students. Then $100 - x$ are males not in Art and $100 - x$ are Art students who are not male. With the 60 outside both:
$$x + (100-x) + (100-x) + 60 = 200 \implies 260 - x = 200 \implies x = 60.$$

**Answer: (C) 60**

prism-2015-09.title: Split into triangles
prism-2015-09.body:
Drawing the two diagonals from one vertex splits the pentagon into 3 triangles, whose angles together make up the pentagon's angles. So the angles of the pentagon sum to $3\times180^\circ = 540^\circ$, and each of the 5 equal angles is $540^\circ\div5 = 108^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $108^\circ$**

prism-2015-09.title: Triangles from the centre
prism-2015-09.body:
Join the centre to all 5 vertices to get 5 congruent isosceles triangles. Each has apex angle $360^\circ\div5 = 72^\circ$, so each base angle is $\frac12(180^\circ - 72^\circ) = 54^\circ$. Each angle of the pentagon is made of two base angles: $2\times54^\circ = 108^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $108^\circ$**

prism-2015-10.title: Worst case
prism-2015-10.body:
The hardest requirement is the blue pair, since blue socks are scarce. In the worst case Peter picks all 10 black socks and only 1 blue sock: 11 socks and still no blue pair. The 12th sock must then be blue, giving a blue pair (and he already has plenty of black). With 11 socks he cannot be sure, so 12 is the minimum.

**Answer: (E) 12**

prism-2015-10.title: Check each requirement
prism-2015-10.body:
To guarantee a black pair he needs at most $4 + 2 = 6$ socks (worst case: all 4 blue first). To guarantee a blue pair he needs $10 + 2 = 12$ socks (worst case: all 10 black first). He must satisfy both, so he needs $\max(6, 12) = 12$.

**Answer: (E) 12**

prism-2015-11.title: Take 100th roots
prism-2015-11.body:
Taking the 100th root (which preserves order for positive numbers): $\sqrt[100]{3^{200}} = 3^2 = 9$, $\sqrt[100]{64^{50}} = 64^{1/2} = 8$, $\sqrt[100]{7^{100}} = 7$. So the order is $7^{100}, 64^{50}, 3^{200}$.

**Answer: (C)**

prism-2015-12.title: Compare squared volumes
prism-2015-12.body:
For a cube of edge $s$, a face diagonal is $s\sqrt2$ and the space diagonal is $s\sqrt3$ (Pythagoras twice: $d^2 = s^2 + 2s^2$).

- (A) $V = 8$, $V^2 = 64$.
- (B) $s = \frac4{\sqrt3}$, $V^2 = s^6 = \frac{4^6}{27} = \frac{4096}{27} \approx 151.7$.
- (C) one face has area $\frac{20}6 = \frac{10}3$, so $V^2 = s^6 = \left(\frac{10}3\right)^3 = \frac{1000}{27} \approx 37$.
- (D) $V^2 = 49$.
- (E) $s = \frac3{\sqrt2}$, $V^2 = \frac{3^6}{8} = \frac{729}8 \approx 91$.

The largest is (B).

**Answer: (B)**

prism-2015-12.title: Compare edge lengths
prism-2015-12.body:
Bigger edge means bigger volume, so compare $s^2$: (A) $4$; (B) $\frac{16}3 \approx 5.33$; (C) $\frac{10}3 \approx 3.33$; (D) $s^3 = 7 < 8$, so $s < 2$, $s^2 < 4$; (E) $\frac92 = 4.5$. The cube in (B) has the longest edge.

**Answer: (B)**

prism-2015-13.title: Use times
prism-2015-13.body:
Let the hill be $d$ km and the downhill speed $s$. Total distance $2d$, total time $\frac d{30} + \frac ds$. Average speed:
$$\frac{2d}{\frac d{30}+\frac ds} = 40 \implies \frac2{\frac1{30}+\frac1s} = 40 \implies \frac1{30}+\frac1s = \frac1{20} \implies \frac1s = \frac1{60}.$$
So $s = 60$ km/h; the distance $d$ cancels.

**Answer: (D) 60 km/h**

prism-2015-13.title: Pick a convenient distance
prism-2015-13.body:
Since the distance cancels, try $d = 60$ km. Uphill takes 2 hours. An average of 40 km/h over 120 km means 3 hours in total, so downhill takes 1 hour: $60$ km/h. (The average speed is the harmonic mean of the two speeds, not the ordinary mean.)

**Answer: (D) 60 km/h**

prism-2015-14.title: Square the difference
prism-2015-14.body:
Squaring $x - y = 10$ gives $x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = 100$. Since $xy = 5$, $x^2 + y^2 = 100 + 2\times5 = 110$.

**Answer: (E) 110**

prism-2015-15.title: Set up speeds
prism-2015-15.body:
Let the boat's still-water speed be $x$ and the water's speed $w$. The distance is $2(x+w) = 3(x-w)$, so $x = 5w$ and the distance is $2(5w + w) = 12w$. In still water the trip takes $\frac{12w}{5w} = \frac{12}5$ hours.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{12}5$**

prism-2015-15.title: Fractions of the trip per hour
prism-2015-15.body:
Downstream the boat covers $\frac12$ of $AB$ per hour, upstream $\frac13$. These are (boat + current) and (boat − current), so the boat alone covers the average, $\frac12\left(\frac12+\frac13\right) = \frac5{12}$ of $AB$ per hour. The trip takes $\frac{12}5$ hours.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{12}5$**

prism-2015-16.title: Inclusion–exclusion
prism-2015-16.body:
Multiples of 4: $\lfloor1000/4\rfloor = 250$. Multiples of 6: $\lfloor1000/6\rfloor = 166$. Numbers divisible by both are the multiples of $\text{lcm}(4,6) = 12$: $\lfloor1000/12\rfloor = 83$; they were counted twice. Total: $250 + 166 - 83 = 333$.

**Answer: (D) 333**

prism-2015-16.title: Count in blocks of 12
prism-2015-16.body:
In each block of 12 consecutive numbers, the ones divisible by 4 or 6 are (for $1$ to $12$) $4, 6, 8, 12$: 4 numbers. $1000 = 83\times12 + 4$, so the 83 full blocks give $332$, and the leftover $997$–$1000$ contains one more ($1000$, divisible by 4). Total $333$.

**Answer: (D) 333**

prism-2015-17.title: Digit sums
prism-2015-17.body:
9 is divisible by 9. $3^{100} - 27 = 9(3^{98} - 3)$ is divisible by 9. (D) is a power of 9. A number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is: (C) has digit sum $2(1+2+\cdots+8) + 9 = 81$, divisible by 9; (E) has digit sum $7\times2 + 7\times7 + 1 = 64$, not divisible by 9.

**Answer: (E)**

prism-2015-17.title: Remainder check for (E)
prism-2015-17.body:
Work out (E) modulo 9 by its digit sum: $64 = 7\times9 + 1$, so (E) leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9. The other four are multiples of 9 as shown (for (B), $3^{100}$ and $27$ are both multiples of 9).

**Answer: (E)**

prism-2015-18.title: The solids don't change
prism-2015-18.body:
Only water evaporates, so there is still 1 kg of solids. Now water is 98% of the mass, so the solids are 2% of the mass. If 2% is 1 kg, then 100% is $1 \div 0.02 = 50$ kg.

**Answer: (C) 50 kg**

prism-2015-18.title: Equation for water lost
prism-2015-18.body:
Suppose $w$ kg of water evaporates. Then $\frac{99-w}{100-w} = \frac{98}{100}$, so $9900 - 100w = 9800 - 98w$, giving $2w = 100$, $w = 50$. The load now weighs $100 - 50 = 50$ kg.

**Answer: (C) 50 kg**

prism-2015-19.title: Follow the wife
prism-2015-19.body:
The 10 minutes saved is the time the wife would have spent driving from the meeting point to the airport and back. So the one-way drive from the meeting point to the airport takes 5 minutes. She would have reached the airport at 9:00, so she met Sean at 8:55. He had been walking since 8:00, so he walked for 55 minutes.

**Answer: (E) 55 minutes**

prism-2015-19.title: Why the other details don't matter
prism-2015-19.body:
The wife left home at the usual time and drove at her usual speed until she met Sean, then turned back. Her round trip was shortened by twice the distance from the meeting point to the airport, which costs 10 minutes of driving — 5 each way. Hence the meeting was 5 minutes before 9 pm, regardless of how fast Sean walks or how far the house is. 8:00 to 8:55 is 55 minutes.

**Answer: (E) 55 minutes**

prism-2015-20.title: Use Antonia
prism-2015-20.body:
The late sister said “I am Tosia”, so she isn't Antonia (who never lies). Antonia is therefore one of the other two, and she tells the truth about who was late. Her answer is either “Antonia was late” (impossible — Antonia wasn't late) or “Dara was late”. So Antonia said “Dara was late”, and it is true. (Tosia then lied that Antonia was late, which she may do.)

**Answer: (B) Dara**

prism-2015-20.title: Test each case
prism-2015-20.body:
- Antonia late: she would have said “I am Tosia”, a lie — impossible.
- Tosia late: the other two are Antonia and Dara; Antonia would truthfully say “Tosia was late”, but nobody said that — impossible.
- Dara late: Dara lies “I am Tosia” ✔; Antonia truthfully says “Dara was late” ✔; Tosia says “Antonia was late”, a lie she is allowed to tell ✔.

Only Dara works.

**Answer: (B) Dara**
